passages.where: The book's first lesson is a father and a mother speaking to a son about to meet the world. The note says the father warns him against a gang that ambushes the innocent for plunder. Proverbs knows that the pull of the group is strongest in the young, and it answers with a parent's voice, not a rulebook.

The father tells his son not to despise the LORD's discipline, because God corrects the one he loves as a father corrects the son he delights in. Discipline here is the shape of delight, not its absence. A teenager who is corrected and still knows he is delighted in can bear a great deal.

Paul tells children to obey their parents and, in the very next breath, tells fathers not to provoke their children, so they will not become discouraged. The parent's authority comes with a limit attached. Constant criticism, unfairness and contempt can break a young spirit as surely as neglect.

Joseph is seventeen, and his father loves him more than his brothers and dresses him to show it. The site's note says Jacob repeated his own father's favoritism, now with twelve sons watching, and that children see the rankings in a family even when no one says them aloud. The brothers' hatred was their own sin, and the father's favoritism fed it.

The second stanza of the longest psalm asks the question every young person faces in some form: how can a young man keep his way pure? The answer is not a set of walls around him but a word hidden in his heart. The singer prays it for himself; he is not only being told.

The Teacher tells the young to rejoice in their youth and follow their heart, and in the same sentence to know that God will bring them to judgment. He does not set joy and accountability against each other. Youth is to be enjoyed, and it is also brief.

Paul tells Timothy, a young leader, not to let anyone look down on his youth, but to set an example for the whole church in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Scripture expects real faithfulness from the young, and does not treat them as Christians in waiting.

When God calls Jeremiah, the prophet protests that he is only a youth. God overrules him: do not say that, but go where I send you and speak what I command, and do not be afraid. The note says God had known and appointed him before he was born. God's call does not wait for a person to feel grown.

John encourages every age group in the church. To the young he says they are strong, the word of God lives in them, and they have overcome the evil one. The church's oldest letters speak to young people as people with real strength and a real fight.

The younger son asks for his share of the estate now, and the father divides his property and lets him go. The note points out that the father gives the older son his share as well. Jesus' story shows a father who does not hold a grown son by force, and who is waiting on the road when he returns.

misread.taken: Obey your parents is sometimes used to demand that a teenager do whatever a parent says, without question, and in the worst cases to keep a child quiet about what is happening at home.
misread.says: Paul says obey your parents in the Lord. The site's note on the chapter explains that a child's obedience belongs to Christ first, so no parent can command what Christ forbids, and that in the very next verse Paul limits the parent: do not provoke your children to anger. The note is plain that these words must never be used to keep a child quiet about abuse or to send a child back to someone who is hurting them.

whole: The teenage years can feel like losing a child you still see every day. The one who used to tell you everything goes quiet. Doors close. A phone holds a world you cannot see, and friends you barely know seem to matter more than you do. Some teenagers argue about everything, and some stop arguing because they have stopped expecting to be heard. Parents swing between holding on harder and giving up, and Christian parents often carry a sharper fear underneath: that their child's faith will not survive these years.

Scripture is not surprised by any of this. Its wisdom literature was written largely for the young, by parents who knew the pull of the group and the hunger of the heart. It is honest about families where favoritism bred hatred, and about a son who took his share and left. It also treats young people as people: God called Jeremiah while he was protesting that he was only a youth, Paul told Timothy to let no one look down on him, and John told the young that they were strong. Much of the trouble in these years comes from a parent and a teenager both forgetting that last point, the parent treating a near adult as a small child and the teenager treating a parent as an obstacle.

So the Bible's wisdom is a slow handing over. Keep speaking, as the father of Proverbs does, with reasons and not only rules, and keep listening longer than feels comfortable. Correct, because correction is love, but do not provoke: discipline that is fair, explained and free of contempt keeps a young person's heart open, and favoritism or constant criticism closes it. Let them carry real responsibility and real faith of their own, because the goal is not a compliant teenager but an adult who can stand before God without you. And pray for them as people God has known before you did, which also means letting them make some choices you would not make.

The hope here is the father on the road. He did not chase his son into the far country, and he did not stop watching for him. Many teenagers come through these years closer to God than their parents feared; some wander and come back; some wander longer. In every case, a parent's love and a parent's prayers matter, and in every case the child's story belongs finally to the God who loves them more than any parent can. A parent can do the next faithful thing and leave the ending with him.
sit: When did your teenager last feel delighted in by you, not just corrected or managed, and what would it take to give them that this week?

prayer.lead: A prayer of someone taught by God from youth, asking to pass that on to the next generation. A parent can pray it for themselves and for their child.

careLines.text: No one may use ‘obey your parents’ to keep a child quiet about abuse, or to send a child back to someone who is hurting them.
Abuse of a child is a crime.
If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now.
If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
